title: Enthalpy, Entropy and Non-Equilibrium Reactions | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Explain why burning glucose and photosynthesis stay away from equilibrium, using the signs of the enthalpy change and the entropy change. Read the sign of the Gibbs free energy change (delta G) to decide whether a reaction is favoured, and keep that separate from how fast it runs. Work through the glucose example one step at a time, then compare the reverse process, photosynthesis.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports analysing non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy.

"analyse examples of non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy, for example:
- combustion reactions
- photosynthesis"

Prerequisite: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, exothermic and endothermic reactions, entropy as the spread of particles and energy, and the link between enthalpy, entropy and delta G. Next: What a flask already at equilibrium does when it is disturbed by a change in concentration or temperature.

Handle equal gas counts and solids, and tell a squeeze apart from adding an inert gas at fixed volume.

description:
A catalyst makes a reaction faster, so why does it not give more product at equilibrium? Distinguish the product formed in a limited time from the amount present at equilibrium, and state what a catalyst does to a mixture that is already at equilibrium.

description:
When a settled mixture changes all of its amounts, the ratio of concentrations stays the same at a fixed temperature. Name that ratio K and write its expression for a reaction in solution from a balanced equation, using coefficients as powers and leaving out solids and pure liquids. Sequence reproduction in flowering plants from pollination to seed, and explain why pollination is not yet fertilisation. Explain how a pollen tube carries sperm to the egg. Name vegetative propagation as the asexual route in plants, then match each route to the conditions where it works best.

description:
Trace a human pregnancy from fertilisation in the oviduct, through cleavage and the blastocyst, to implantation in a uterine lining that progesterone has prepared. description:

description:
Unwound, the DNA in one human cell would be about two metres long. See how cells store it. Bacteria keep one circular chromosome in the nucleoid, coiled and held by proteins, plus small plasmids that can pass between cells. Eukaryotes keep linear chromosomes in a nucleus, wound on histones into chromatin that loosens to read genes and tightens for division. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA, a clue to where they came from.

Follow an ionic solid as it enters water. Polar water molecules pull ions off the crystal surface and surround them, a process called hydration. title: Punnett Squares and Pedigrees | Year 12 Biology
description:
Two tall parents, one short offspring: how? Learn dominant and recessive alleles, homozygous and heterozygous genotypes, and how a Punnett square gives the chance for each child, not a guaranteed count. Then read a pedigree to decide whether a trait is dominant or recessive, using the clues that settle it.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports constructing and interpreting pedigrees and Punnett squares.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis, including but not limited to: interpreting examples of autosomal, sex-linkage, co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles (ACSBL085); constructing and interpreting information and data from pedigrees and Punnett squares"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Meiosis and sources of genetic variation. Next: Sex linkage, co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles.
